newsitem.title: USA: Dictaphone Corp hangs future on new product line.
newsitem.headline: Dictaphone Corp hangs future on new product line.

text.p: Dictaphone Corp, the century-old company founded by an associate of Alexander Graham Bell, says it is staking its future on a group of new products that rely on sophisticated voice recognition technology and Windows-based programs.
If the new products -- mostly for hospitals, courtrooms and call centers -- take off, company officials and analysts said an initial public offering may very well follow.
"With a year or two of good growth they could go public," said David Allen, an analyst at Morgan Stanley.

The Stratford, Conn.-based company, sold by Pitney Bowes Inc in 1995 to Stonington Partners for $462 million, has doubled its R&D budget this year to $18 million and plans to unveil 12 new products in 18 months.
"Since the divestiture from Pitney Bowes we have invested a lot of money in R&D, marketing and getting our products to this stage," said Joe Skrzypczak, chief financial officer.
Dictaphone's chief executive and chairman, John Duerden, said he is sure the company's recent investments will pay off soon.
"The company grew about 2 percent a year," Duerden said. "I would expect to be growing in the double digits in the next three to four years."
But the first step for the market leader is to maneuver through a difficult transition, saddled with debt and only just starting to ship the latest products.
A Standard & Poor's credit review in May rated the company's outlook as negative because it is highy leveraged and faces substantial loan amortization requirements.

As of March 31, the company had outstanding term loans of $139.5 million and a $22.25 million loan outstanding under a $40 million revolving credit facility. It also had $200 million of notes outstanding, according to financial reports.
Scott Levy, a Banker's Trust analyst, said Dictaphone had been the "200-pound gorilla" with its products falling behind the competition, until recently.
"They are rolling out all these new products, they are looking forward to a strong fourth quarter. All the big bondholders are waiting for that," Levy said.
Duerden, who declined to comment on the company's upcoming quarterly results, said this year was indeed critical for the company.

"This year is the pivotal year for us, to go from where we came and to where we are going," he said. "I really believe we've got the ball at the top of the hill. I think the concept that we've got is the right one."

He pointed to several new products the company is banking on, including the Enterprise Express system, a Windows-based voice processing system that allows doctors' dictated reports to be managed through voice or text files.
Dictaphone recently won a contract with the D.C. Superior Court to install a digital audio court recording system, a product that helps manage digital testimony.
Levy said the company's strong brand recognition and well-established distribution network should help pull Dictaphone through this transition.
"I think it will work but I think there will be some hiccups," he said. "They are in the right business at the right time."

For the first quarter of this year, Dictaphone posted an operating loss of $1.1 million on revenues of $81.2 million compared to an operating loss of $7.1 million on $80.5 million of revenues last year.
((-- New York Newsdesk, 212-859-1610))
